notes: Rules are sorted by ascending tier first, then descending priority. The first rule whose `when` block fully matches is selected. Tier 1 always overrides. Empty `when` matches everything (fallback).

rules.label: Immediate physical danger
why: You indicated you are in immediate physical danger. That takes precedence over everything else in this system.
Emergency services are the correct first contact when physical safety is at risk.
Digital reporting can wait. Physical safety cannot.
actions: Call 112 now if you are in danger.
Move to a safe location if you can do so without further risk.
Tell one person you trust where you are.
Do not attempt to handle the digital situation until you are safe.
evidence: Once safe, preserve any threatening messages or call logs
Note the date, time, and location of the threat
Keep a record of who you contacted and when

rules.label: NCII — Minor subject, active threat
why: A person under 18 is involved, so this routes through child-protection channels.
An active threat makes this time-sensitive — evidence and reporting are most effective in the first 24 hours.
Take It Down (NCMEC) is built specifically for under-18 cases and uses hash-based blocking.
actions: Do not delete the images, posts, or messages. They are your record.
Do not pay and do not negotiate. Payment confirms the threat works.
File with Take It Down (NCMEC) — built for under-18 cases.
File on NCRP and save the acknowledgement number.
Report the content inside the platform, quoting your NCRP number.
evidence: Direct URLs of every post, profile, or album hosting the content
Screenshots showing the content, uploader handle, and timestamp
Every message containing a demand, threat, or deadline
Your NCRP acknowledgement number once filed

rules.label: NCII — Minor subject
why: A person under 18 is involved, so Take It Down (NCMEC) is the correct takedown service.
Hash-based blocking prevents re-uploads without your image ever being uploaded.
An NCRP complaint creates the official record both the platform and police will reference.
actions: Do not delete the original images, posts, or messages.
File with Take It Down (NCMEC).
File on NCRP and save the acknowledgement number.
Report the content on each platform and reference your Take It Down case.
evidence: Direct URLs of every post, profile, or album hosting the content
Screenshots showing the content, uploader handle, and timestamp
Your Take It Down case reference and NCRP acknowledgement number

rules.label: NCII — Active blackmail or extortion
why: An active threat makes this time-sensitive. Do not pay — payment does not end extortion.
StopNCII.org generates a hash on your own device so participating platforms can block re-uploads.
An NCRP complaint produces the written record that both the platform and police will ask for.
actions: Do not pay. Do not engage. Do not negotiate.
Do not delete anything — the messages are your evidence.
Create a hash case at StopNCII.org from your own device.
File on NCRP and keep the acknowledgement number.
evidence: Every message containing a demand, threat, or deadline
Direct URLs of every post, profile, or album hosting the content
Screenshots showing the content, uploader handle, and timestamp
Your StopNCII case reference and NCRP acknowledgement number

rules.label: Stalking or harassment — ongoing
why: The behaviour is ongoing, so personal-safety steps come before platform or legal steps.
An NCRP complaint filed while the conduct is live is stronger than one filed after it stops.
This route records a pattern rather than a single incident.
actions: Tell one person you trust where you are and what is happening.
Stop responding. Do not engage, negotiate, or explain.
Log every incident with date, time, and platform.
File on NCRP and keep the acknowledgement number.
If there is any threat of physical harm, call 112.
evidence: A dated log of every incident — date, time, platform, what happened
Screenshots of messages, calls, and profile activity
Accounts, handles, and phone numbers used
Names of anyone who witnessed similar contact

rules.label: UPI fraud — money already transferred
why: Money has already moved. Speed matters more than completeness — the first hours give the best chance of a freeze.
1930 is the national cyber-fraud financial helpline. A report there triggers bank-level action.
The NCRP complaint produces the written record your bank and police will ask for.
actions: Call 1930 now. Do not wait until you have gathered everything.
Block your UPI ID in your banking app.
Ask your bank to flag the transaction and the beneficiary account.
File on NCRP the same day and note the acknowledgement number.
Do not pay any recovery fee to anyone offering to get the money back.
evidence: Transaction IDs, UTR numbers, and bank statements showing the debit
The beneficiary UPI ID or account number
Full chat or call history with the person who contacted you
Screenshots of the offer or listing that started it

rules.label: Financial fraud — money already transferred
why: Money has already moved. The first hours give the best chance of a freeze at the receiving bank.
1930 is the national cyber-fraud helpline — a report there triggers bank-level action.
The NCRP complaint produces the written record your bank and police will ask for.
actions: Call 1930 immediately.
Contact your bank's fraud line and ask them to flag the transaction.
File on NCRP the same day and keep the acknowledgement number.
Do not pay any recovery fee to anyone offering to get the money back.
evidence: Transaction IDs, UTR numbers, and bank statements showing the debit
The beneficiary account or UPI ID
Every message or call from the person who contacted you
Screenshots of the fake listing, job offer, or investment page

rules.label: Content you created, being reposted without consent
why: You created the content, so a copyright (DMCA) takedown is the fastest removal channel.
DMCA requires a signed declaration and the original URL, both of which you control.
If the content is intimate and being used to threaten you, StopNCII.org is also available.
actions: File a DMCA takedown with the platform's copyright form.
Include the URL, your original file, and a signed declaration.
If not removed within 48 hours, escalate to the platform's Trust and Safety team.
If there is a threat attached, create a StopNCII case and file on NCRP.
evidence: The original file and its metadata
The URL where your content is being reposted
Screenshots of the reposting account and timestamp
Your DMCA submission reference

rules.label: NCII — Non-consensual intimate image
why: The subject is an adult, so StopNCII.org is the correct takedown service.
Hash-based blocking prevents re-uploads without your image being uploaded anywhere.
An NCRP complaint in parallel gives you a written record to escalate with.
actions: Do not delete the original files or messages.
Create a hash case at StopNCII.org from your own device.
File on NCRP and keep the acknowledgement number.
Report the content on each platform and reference your StopNCII case.
evidence: Direct URLs of every post, profile, or album hosting the content
Screenshots showing the content, uploader handle, and timestamp
Any message containing a demand or threat
Your StopNCII case reference and NCRP acknowledgement number

rules.label: Phishing — attempt only, no money lost
why: No transfer has happened, so this route prioritises blocking the attempt before it completes.
CERT-In is the correct escalation for phishing infrastructure.
Reporting on NCRP records the attempt even when nothing was lost.
actions: Do not click any further links or download any attachments.
Change your passwords from a different, trusted device.
Forward the phishing email or message to reportphishing@cert-in.org.in.
Report the attempt on NCRP so it is on record.
evidence: The full email headers or the message thread
Screenshots of the phishing page
The URL, sender address, or phone number used
A note of the date and time you received it

rules.label: Financial fraud — attempt only
why: No transfer has happened yet, so this route prioritises blocking the attempt.
Reporting on NCRP records the attempt even when nothing was lost.
CERT-In is the right escalation if the attempt came through a compromised link or device.
actions: Do not complete any pending payment.
Share no further OTP, PIN, or CVV.
Report the number, UPI ID, or listing on NCRP.
Warn your bank and ask them to watch the account.
evidence: The phone numbers, UPI IDs, or profiles used to contact you
Screenshots of the offer, listing, or message thread
Call logs and message timestamps

rules.label: Account takeover
why: The account is compromised, so regaining control comes before anything is reported.
CERT-In is the correct escalation for account compromise.
An NCRP filing documents the compromise in case the account was used to commit fraud.
actions: Change the password from a different, trusted device.
Enable two-factor authentication, then revoke all active sessions.
Check and revert any recovery email, phone number, or forwarding rule the attacker added.
Warn your contacts that the account may have sent messages on your behalf.
File on NCRP; notify CERT-In if a work account is involved.
evidence: The time you first noticed the compromise
Any new login or password changed alert emails
Messages or posts sent from the account that you did not send
The attacker's recovery email or phone number, if added

rules.label: Account locked or suspended
why: This is a platform-level action, so the platform's own appeal process is the correct first step.
Having proof of ownership ready speeds up the appeal considerably.
If the lock was triggered by someone else's action, an NCRP filing records it.
actions: Check your email for the reason for the lock or suspension.
Prepare an appeal with proof of identity and ownership.
Contact platform support through the official appeal process.
Enable 2FA once the account is restored.
File on NCRP if you believe the lock was triggered by someone else.
evidence: The email or notification you received about the lock
Any identity documents the platform has previously accepted
The date the lock started and any case number the platform gave you

rules.label: Account issue — general
why: The account is affected but the exact type is unclear, so this route starts with the recovery basics.
CERT-In is the correct escalation if compromise is confirmed.
An NCRP filing documents the incident if the account was used to harm others.
actions: Change the password from a different, trusted device.
Enable two-factor authentication and revoke any sessions you do not recognise.
Review linked apps and remove anything unfamiliar.
File on NCRP if the account was used to commit fraud or harassment.
evidence: The date you first noticed unusual activity
Any security alert emails
Screenshots of activity you did not authorise
The platform's case reference, if one was given

rules.label: Stalking or harassment — not ongoing
why: The conduct is not currently ongoing, so this route prioritises building a complete record.
NCRP accepts pattern-based complaints — one detailed filing is stronger than scattered reports.
Reporting puts the conduct on record, which matters if it restarts.
actions: Write out a single timeline of everything that happened, with dates.
File one NCRP complaint covering the full pattern.
Keep the originals — do not delete messages even if you have blocked the person.
If it restarts, file an update referencing your existing complaint number.
evidence: Your written timeline covering the full period
Screenshots of messages, calls, and profile activity
Accounts, handles, and phone numbers used
Any prior complaint or acknowledgement numbers

rules.label: General cybercrime route
why: Your answers did not match a specific crisis pattern, so this falls back to the general reporting route.
NCRP is the single entry point for all cybercrime categories in India.
actions: File on NCRP describing what happened in your own words.
Keep every message, screenshot, and reference number.
If money was involved, call 1930.
evidence: Screenshots of everything relevant
Any reference numbers you have been given
A short written timeline of events
